vignette:
He is 52, a South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life working with his hands. For more than two decades, he has been an HVAC technician, the kind of person who notices the sound a failing motor makes before anyone else does, who can tell by smell if something is overheating. He takes pride in being steady, dependable, and practical. His wife describes him as someone who used to come home tired but satisfied, still joking with the children over dinner, still willing to fix a loose cabinet hinge before bed.

The event happens on an ordinary workday. He is called to service a commercial cooling system in an older building. He remembers the mechanical room as cramped, hot, and poorly ventilated. At first he thinks he is dealing with a routine refrigerant leak, something unpleasant but manageable. Then there is a sharp chemical odor, stronger than expected, and almost immediately his eyes begin to burn. He feels it in his throat and chest next, an invading sensation that turns breathing into work. He tries to shut off the system and back out of the room, but his body begins to panic before his mind can catch up. He coughs hard, stumbles, and feels a wave of dizziness so sudden that he has to grab a pipe to stay upright. In the confusion he is aware of one thought repeating itself with unusual clarity: I am not getting enough air.

He is taken to the emergency department, where the hours feel unreal and stretched thin. He remembers oxygen tubing, the sting in his lungs, and the fear that each breath might not be enough. Even after he is medically stabilized and sent home, the experience does not end. For weeks he is preoccupied with his breathing. Any tightness in his chest feels like the beginning of another disaster. He checks the air in rooms as soon as he enters them. He opens windows even in bad weather. He asks his wife if she smells anything strange. He begins carrying a mask and repeatedly inspects the filters in his own home, unable to trust what once felt familiar.

When he first returns to work, he tells himself he is lucky to still have a job and that a skilled technician cannot be afraid of equipment rooms. But the body he relies on no longer behaves the way it used to. The hiss of pressurized gas makes his shoulders jerk. The smell of cleaning solvents, refrigerants, or burnt dust causes his stomach to drop before he can reason with himself. In basements and enclosed utility spaces he feels trapped, suddenly aware of every breath. He starts avoiding certain service calls and inventing practical excuses to trade assignments with coworkers. If he cannot avoid them, he rushes, skips steps, and then criticizes himself afterward for being careless. He used to be known for patience and precision. Now he second-guesses gauges, rereads safety labels over and over, and still leaves feeling unsure.

At night the event returns in fragments. He wakes coughing, convinced for a few seconds that the chemical smell is in the bedroom. Sometimes he dreams that he is back in the mechanical room and the door will not open. His wife says he thrashes and grabs at his throat in sleep. He does not like talking about these nights. He becomes embarrassed by how frightened he feels and begins sleeping later than she does so he will not disturb her. During the day he is tired and irritable. Small inconveniences—a traffic delay, a misplaced tool, a customer asking too many questions—can bring a flash of anger that surprises even him.

He notices himself changing at home as much as at work. He no longer enjoys grilling because smoke and fumes make him uneasy. He avoids crowded indoor places, especially restaurants with strong kitchen smells. Family members invite him to gatherings, but he often declines, saying he is too busy or too tired. He spends more time alone in the garage, cleaning and reorganizing tools that do not need attention. It is one of the few places where he feels some control. His wife tries to reassure him, but he hears concern in her voice and interprets it as disappointment. He worries that he has become weak, though he would never use that word for anyone else.

What troubles him most is that the world now feels contaminated in ways it never did before. He scans ceilings for vents, listens for compressors cycling on, and notices odors other people ignore. He says he used to walk into buildings thinking about the job; now he walks in thinking about escape routes. He knows, logically, that not every machine room is dangerous. He knows he survived. But his body does not live by logic. Months later, he is still living as if the air around him might suddenly turn against him again.
